text:
The rollout started at nine in the morning and looked healthy for the first hour. Error rates were flat, latency was flat, and the canary was taking ten percent of traffic without complaint. We widened it to half, and that is when the first reports came in from the mobile team.

What changed at fifty percent was not the code but the connection pool. At ten percent the new build shared a pool with the old one and stayed well under the ceiling. At half it had its own pool, sized from a config default that nobody had revisited since the service was a third of the size.

The rollback was slower than it should have been. The deploy tool will not roll back while a canary analysis is running, and the analysis was stuck because it was waiting for metrics from instances that had already been replaced. We waited eleven minutes for a timeout that we could have skipped with a flag none of us knew about.

The fix for the pool is a one line change and it is already merged. The fix for the rollback is a documentation change and an argument about whether the tool should have that behaviour at all, and I would rather have that argument than write the runbook entry.
note: Four paragraphs in two sections of two, the first case in this file where a heading is earned.

text:
Storage is the part of this design that has an obvious answer and a correct one, and they are different. The obvious answer is to put the transcripts in the same database as everything else, because it is already backed up, already monitored, and already has a schema migration story. That works until someone dictates for an hour and we are storing a megabyte of text per row in a database sized for kilobytes.

The correct answer is that transcripts are files. They are written once, read rarely, and superseded rather than edited, and their natural unit is the session. Putting them on disk with a pointer in the row gives us cheap writes, cheap reads and a backup story that is a directory copy.

Retention is where this gets political rather than technical. The product position is that nothing leaves the device, so retention is the user's problem and the app should not have an opinion. The support position is that a user who deletes a transcript by accident will ask us to get it back.

I think both are right and that the resolution is a bin rather than a policy. A deleted transcript moves to a folder the app clears on a schedule the user sets, which means we have not stored anything they did not ask us to store, and we have not thrown anything away the moment they clicked the wrong thing.
note: Two named sections that earn headings while the peer looking triads inside stay prose.

text:
Installation is a single file and no installer service. The setup program writes into your user profile, registers a startup entry if you ask it to, and leaves Program Files alone, which is why it works on a locked down machine where you cannot elevate.

If your organisation blocks unsigned downloads you will need the package from the Store instead. It is the same build with a different signature — the settings folder is shared — so moving between the two keeps your dictionary and your history.

Updating happens in the background and lands on the next restart of the app. There is no forced restart and no nagging dialog, because an app that interrupts you to talk about itself is worse than an app that is one version behind.

If you want the update now, the tray menu has an item that applies the downloaded package immediately. It restarts the app, keeps your settings, and takes about as long as opening it normally does.
protectedTokens: a different signature — the settings folder is shared —

text:
The estimate was wrong in the way estimates are usually wrong, which is to say it was right about the work we knew about. Six weeks was a fair number for the migration as it was described in January, and by March the description had changed twice without the number changing once.

I am not arguing for bigger estimates. I am arguing that the number should have been re-cut when the scope moved, and that the reason it was left alone is that re-cutting an estimate feels like admitting the first one was bad.

The scope moved for good reasons both times. The first change came from a security review that we asked for, and the second came from a customer commitment that predated the project and surfaced late because the person who made it had moved teams.

Neither of those is a failure of planning. The failure is that both were absorbed silently, so the plan on the wall and the work in flight described different projects for most of February.
note: Long retrospective in two sections, connected throughout, with a spelled out duration.

text:
Why the queue looks empty. The consumer reads with a visibility timeout of thirty seconds, and the metric the dashboard graphs is the count of messages available to receive, which excludes anything currently invisible. A healthy consumer therefore keeps the graph near zero even when it is behind, because the messages are in flight rather than waiting.

The number you actually want is the age of the oldest message, which the API exposes as ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage. It goes up when you are falling behind and it comes down when you catch up, and it does not care how the work is split between waiting and in flight.

Why the alarm did not fire. The alarm was written against the available count with a threshold of a thousand, and the available count stayed under a thousand because the consumers were picking messages up promptly and then failing to process them. Each failure returned the message to the queue after the visibility timeout, so the same work went round repeatedly while the graph stayed calm.

Rewriting the alarm against oldest message age would have caught it in about a minute. That is the change I have made, and I have left the old alarm in place for a fortnight so we can watch the two disagree.
note: The author supplies both section names, so the headings are not invented, and one identifier wants code.

text:
The first week was about the walking and the second was about the weather, and I would not have guessed that in advance. We had planned the route around distance, so the days were even on paper and wildly uneven underfoot, because a flat ten kilometres on a farm track and a flat ten kilometres across a bog are the same number and not the same day.

By the fourth evening we had stopped reading the distances and started reading the surface, which is the sort of thing everyone tells you beforehand and nobody understands until their feet do.

The weather turned on the Tuesday and stayed turned. Rain in that part of the country is not dramatic, it is administrative: it arrives at a steady rate, it fills in the gaps in your kit that you had been getting away with, and it makes every decision about stopping into a decision about whether you will get warm again.

We finished a day early, which felt like defeat at the time and reads like sense now. The last section was the one we had been looking forward to, and doing it cold, wet and rushed would have turned the good part of the trip into the part we remembered.
note: Long personal narrative that is four paragraphs of one story, so no heading and no list.

text:
Take-home exercises. We stopped sending them because the completion rate told us who had a free weekend rather than who could do the job, and the people we most wanted were the ones least able to spend six hours on spec work.

What replaced them is a paired session on our own code, in a branch we throw away afterwards. It is harder to standardise and it is much better evidence, because we watch how someone reads code they did not write, which is most of the job.

Reference calls. We still do them and we do them late, after the offer is drafted, because a reference call before the decision tends to become a search for permission rather than a search for information.

The questions are the same every time and the useful one is the last: would you work with this person again, and what would you want them to be doing? A hesitation there has changed our mind twice, and both times the hesitation was the whole content of the answer.
